title: Cap. 5 Mem. 2 Obj. 2: No injury when the gospel binds the fruit to faith
pass_a_gloss: If after the accepted sufficient ransom (λυτρον) God does not receive all into grace, he would be injurious to Christ, because he does not grant to humans what Christ by dying merited for them: he would also act unjustly with humans, because he still holds them bound by sins as by debts, whose all debts Christ wiped out (dispunxit) by his blood. Injury is brought upon neither. Not upon Christ, because he himself did not will that the satisfaction performed by him for the sins of the human race should avail for the actual reconciliation of singular humans except with their faith intervening, as was proved above. It would therefore be contumelious to Christ if anyone were admitted into the society and actual participation of this grace not yet believing in the Author of salvation and our Redeemer Jesus Christ. Nor is injury brought upon humans in that they are not received at once into God's favor because of the very act of Christ dying, because this was neither owed to humans nor promised. For we cannot claim for ourselves from Christ's death any benefit against or beyond the order and pact constituted by God and Christ and laid open to us in the Gospel. But this order has been established, this condition expressly set in the Gospel, that the grace of reconciliation and the benefit of eternal life would overflow to sinners from Christ's death if they believed; but if not, they would remain bound by sins and perish in their unbelief: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him (John 3:36).
pass_b_english: Suppose that after accepting a sufficient ransom God still does not receive everyone into grace. Then, the objection says, he would wrong Christ, because he would not grant to human beings what Christ merited for them by dying. He would also deal unjustly with human beings, because he would still hold them bound by sins as by debts, even though Christ wiped out all those debts with his blood.

Neither side is injured. Not Christ: he himself did not will that the satisfaction he offered for the sins of the human race should avail for the actual reconciliation of particular persons unless their faith intervened, as we proved above. It would therefore be an insult to Christ if anyone were admitted into the actual fellowship and share of this grace while still not believing in Jesus Christ, the Author of salvation and our Redeemer. Nor are human beings injured when they are not received at once into God's favor simply on account of Christ's dying act, for that was neither owed to them nor promised. We cannot claim from Christ's death any benefit against or beyond the order and covenant established by God and by Christ and opened to us in the Gospel.

That order stands fixed, and the Gospel expressly sets this condition: the grace of reconciliation and the gift of eternal life overflow to sinners from Christ's death if they believe; if they do not, they remain bound by sins and perish in their unbelief. "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, and the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36).
source_text:
Si post acceptatum λυτρον sufficiens Deus non recipiat omnes in gratiam, Christo injurius esset, quia non gratificatur hominibus quod Christus moriendo pro illis meruit: cum hominibus etiam injuste ageret, quia eos peccatis, quasi debitis, constrictos adhuc tenet, quorum omnia debita Christus suo sanguine dispunxit.

Neutri infertur injuria. Non Christo, quia ipse noluit satisfactionem a se praestitam pro peccatis humani generis valere ad actualem reconciliationem hominum singularium, nisi interveniente fide eorundem, ut supra probatum est. Esset igitur Christo contumeliosum, si in societatem & participationem actualem hujus gratiae quilibet admitteretur, nondum credens in Autorem salutis & Redemtorem nostrum Jesum Christum. Neque hominibus infertur injuria, eo quod non recipiantur illico in favorem Dei propter ipsum actum Christi morientis, quia hoc neque debitum fuit hominibus, neque promissum. Non possumus enim ex morte Christi vendicare nobis ullum beneficium contra, aut praeter ordinem ac pactum a Deo Christoque constitutum, nobisque in Evangelio patefactum. Est autem hic ordo stabilitus, haec conditio expresse posita in Evangelio, quod reconciliationis gratia & beneficium vitae aeternae ad peccatores ex morte Christi redundaret, si crederent; sin minus, manerent obstricti peccatis, & perirent in sua infidelitate: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam aeternam; qui vero non obtemperat Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum, Joh. iii. 36.
